assessments.title: Governance Point Finalizes Executive Sheet Week 1 Friday (Step 6)
assessments.quote: On Friday week 1, the Governance Point must make sure that the Executive Sheet is finalized and ready for handover to the Spell Team. This includes verifying that all required fields are completed, the content aligns with decisions made during the GovOps meeting, and all financial details are accurate. The Governance Point must notify the Spell Team in the govops channel in Slack that the Executive Sheet is finalized. Any updates to the Executive Sheet made after Friday, week 1, must follow the procedure in [A.1.10.2.4.8.3.8 - Core Facilitator Must Notify Spell Team Of Changes](e3d137d7-3244-497b-b065-25cc2dffafeb).
assessments.description: Requires the Governance Point to finalize the Executive Sheet by Friday of week 1, verify it, and notify the Spell Team in Slack.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The Friday week 1 deadline, the named actor, and the Slack notification channel are concrete. Verification is delegated to undefined criteria: 'all required fields are completed', 'aligns with decisions', and 'financial details are accurate' have no checklist, metric, or tolerance.
metrics: Executive Sheet finalized by Friday, week 1
Governance Point notifies Spell Team in the govops Slack channel that the sheet is finalized
All required fields completed
Content aligns with GovOps meeting decisions
All financial details accurate
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalogued mechanism reaches a missed Friday deadline or an inaccurate sheet; Agent Artifact Review covers agents rather than this governance-point process, and the cross-referenced notification procedure (e3d137d7) governs post-Friday changes rather than enforcing this rule.

assessments.title: Governance Point Must Ensure The Executive Sheet Is Completed
assessments.quote:
The Governance Point is responsible for ensuring that the Executive Sheet is fully completed and accurate. This includes the following:

- That all fields in the Executive Sheet are filled in with the required information, including URLs, figures, and confirmations. For any incomplete items (e.g., awaiting final figures), they must be marked with a `TODO` tag.
- That all items included in the Executive Sheet were discussed and approved during the GovOps meeting.
    - No approved items from the discussions can be omitted without a valid reason.
- That the financial transfers are accurate.
    - USDS transfers must be rounded up to the nearest whole number (no decimal points).
    - SKY transfers must be listed to exactly two decimal places.
    - Verify that the checksum for USDS and SKY transfers is accurate.
- The Spell items must be listed in order of importance for an average SKY voter except when there are order of operations concerns.
assessments.description: Makes the Governance Point responsible for completing the Executive Sheet, with rounding, checksum, and ordering requirements for transfers and spells.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The transfer rules are concrete: USDS rounded up to a whole number, SKY stated to exactly two decimals, and a checksum check. Completeness, approval, the 'valid reason' exception, and the 'average SKY voter' ordering standard are judgment-based, so the rule is mixed.
metrics: USDS transfers rounded up to the nearest whole number (no decimal points)
SKY transfers listed to exactly two decimal places
Checksum for USDS and SKY transfers verified as accurate
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph describes an internal governance-process duty with no on-chain enforcement, capital at risk, or named enforcer with penalties. Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) targets Agents rather than the Governance Point, and the Reports of Misalignment and Adjudication catch-alls alone are weak.

assessments.title: Summary Checklist
assessments.quote: The checklist found at [https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/blob/main/processes/spell-sheet-review.md](https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/blob/main/processes/spell-sheet-review.md) outlines the items for the finalization process that should be done.
assessments.description: Points to an external GitHub checklist that lists items to complete when finalizing the executive sheet.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph states no thresholds, deadlines, or operative criteria. Its only content is a link to a separate checklist and the word "should", so there is nothing binding in this text to comply with.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No mechanism in the catalog reaches compliance with an executive-sheet finalization checklist. Artifact review (d4bf73e7) covers agent artifacts, and the other security mechanisms do not address this step.

assessments.title: Spell Crafter Crafts Spell Week 2 Monday (Step 7)
assessments.quote: The Spell Crafter must ensure that the Spell is crafted and completed on Monday week 2.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter to ensure the executive spell is crafted and completed by Monday of week 2.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names a defined actor (Spell Crafter) and a deadline (Monday, week 2), but the week anchor is relative and undefined here, with no time of day or time zone. "Crafted and completed" has no objective completion criteria.
metrics: Spell is crafted and completed by Monday of week 2
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No on-chain or named enforcer reaches a missed spell-crafting deadline. Only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply, and this paragraph does not invoke artifact review or penalties.

assessments.title: Spell Crafting Workflow
assessments.quote: In the Development Stage, the Spell Crafter writes the code for the Spell based on the contents of the Executive Sheet. The output of the Development Process is a Pull Request containing the code for the Spell that is ready for review. In performing the Development Stage, the Crafter takes the steps set forth in the checklists found in the Core Spell Crafter Mainnet Workflow, as specified in [A.1.10.2.5.1.3.2.0.6.1 - Registered Spell Checklists](93f5b36b-06a7-4282-9fd7-14e0cbafd08e).
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter to write Spell code from the Executive Sheet, deliver a Pull Request, and follow the registered checklists.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The actor, the input (Executive Sheet), the output (a Pull Request), and the checklist reference are all named. Compliance turns on the judgment phrase "ready for review" and on checklist steps defined elsewhere, with no metric, threshold, or deadline in the text.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps can review the crafter's spell artifacts and checklist adherence and assess penalties, which plausibly reaches a violation of the checklist requirement. The consequence is not quantified for this rule and firing depends on the review being initiated, so it is mid rather than strong.

assessments.title: Previous Spell Code Cleanup
assessments.quote: Before developing the current Spell, the designated Crafter must clean up the previous Spell code. Code cleanup includes the `DssSpell.sol` (Spell code), `DssSpell.t.sol` (Spell code tests) and `config.sol`(deployed Spell information) files. In this process of code cleanup, the Crafter must remove unused interfaces as well as Spell code and test code from the last Spell. If relevant, they must also clean up any dependency files from the previous Spell that are not being used for the current Spell.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter to clean up the previous Spell's code, test, config, and unused dependency files before developing the current Spell.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation names specific files (DssSpell.sol, DssSpell.t.sol, config.sol), a required action (remove unused interfaces and prior Spell code/tests), and a sequencing point (before developing the current Spell). However, the scope of 'unused' dependencies and the 'if relevant' condition are delegated to the Crafter's judgment, so compliance is partly arguable.
metrics: Cleanup must occur before developing the current Spell
Files in scope: DssSpell.sol, DssSpell.t.sol, config.sol, plus unused dependency files if relevant
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, artifact review, or on-chain mechanism reaches a failure to clean up stale spell files; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply, and the cleanup is a self-policed hygiene step.

assessments.title: The Executive Sheet Serves As Source Of Truth
assessments.quote: The Crafter must use the Executive Sheet as their key reference document and source of truth while developing the Spell. While the Executive Document is the instruction document for the Executive Process, the Executive Sheet is available earlier which enables the Crafter to begin Spell development at an earlier stage.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter to use the Executive Sheet as the key reference and source of truth when developing the Spell.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A named actor (the Crafter) and a real obligation are stated, but the obligation is expressed in judgment language ('key reference document', 'source of truth') with no metric, threshold, deadline, or verification method. Compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism reaches a Crafter's use of the Executive Sheet: the artifact review (d4bf73e7) covers Agent artifacts rather than spell development, and no penalty, contract, or emergency path applies. Only the misalignment catch-all (c6c6f595) reaches it.

assessments.title: The Crafter Is The Only Party Permitted To Approve GitHub Suggestions
assessments.quote: The designated Crafter is the only person or entity permitted to commit GitHub code suggestions to the Spell. The Crafter can only commit suggestions that have been made by a designated Reviewer for the particular Spell. However, using GitHub suggestions is generally discouraged while developing the Spell.
assessments.description: Restricts GitHub suggestion commits to the designated Crafter, who may commit only Reviewer-made suggestions for the Spell.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The actors (Crafter, designated Reviewer) and the permission rule are concrete and checkable against commit history. However, the text does not define how a Crafter or Reviewer is designated, sets no cadence, and states the discouragement of suggestions only qualitatively ("generally discouraged").
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No on-chain or access-control mechanism governs GitHub commit permissions. Artifact review (d4bf73e7) covers agent artifacts rather than Spell commits, and the misalignment and adjudication backstops are catch-alls.

assessments.title: Crafter Master Branch Safety Check
assessments.quote: In order to ensure that no malicious maintenance pull requests have been merged, the Crafter must check that the latest commit made to the "master" (or "main") branch of the Spell repository is the commit that merged the last Spell to master.
assessments.description: Requires the Crafter to verify that the latest master or main branch commit is the commit that merged the last Spell.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The check is a concrete, objectively verifiable equality test between the latest commit and the last Spell's merge commit, with a named actor and branch. It gives no cadence or timing for the check and no required action if the commits differ.
metrics: Latest commit on the master (or main) branch of the Spell repository must equal the commit that merged the last Spell to master
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps can review the Crafter's process against its stated checks and assess penalties, so it plausibly reaches a skipped or falsified check. The consequence is not quantified for this specific step, and no mechanism automatically detects a failed check.

assessments.title: Tests Must Pass Before Crafter Provides Spell to Reviewers
assessments.quote: Before marking a Spell’s Pull Request as "ready for review", the Crafter must ensure that both continuous integration tests and locally run tests are all passing successfully. The only exception to this rule is when the continuous integration tests are broken at no fault of the Spell Team - due to a GitHub failure or otherwise - in which case the Spell can be marked as "ready for review" if locally run tests are passing. The Crafter must not remove or disable failing tests in order to bypass this rule.
assessments.description: Requires a Spell Crafter to have CI and local tests passing before marking a Spell PR ready for review, with a narrow CI-outage exception and no test removal.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The gate is objectively checkable: both CI and local test suites must pass before the "ready for review" status, and disabling or removing failing tests is prohibited. The CI-outage exception turns on "no fault of the Spell Team" and "or otherwise", which are open judgment criteria, so the edge condition is not fully defined.
metrics: Continuous integration tests and locally run tests must all be passing before marking a Spell PR "ready for review"
Exception applies only when CI tests are broken at no fault of the Spell Team (e.g., GitHub failure) and locally run tests are passing
Crafter must not remove or disable failing tests to bypass the rule
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps can review spell artifacts, including a PR marked ready with failing tests, and assess penalties. The rule does not specify a penalty, and the review only fires when it reaches this PR, so the consequence is unquantified.

assessments.title: Process For Handling Technical Issues
assessments.quote: The Crafter plays a key role in the process for identifying, analyzing, and resolving technical issues like bugs, mistakes, and exploits when they arise during the Spell development process. Other stakeholders, including the Spell Reviewer and Core Facilitator, also play an important role. This process is set out in the subdocuments herein.
assessments.description: Describes the Crafter's role in identifying and resolving technical issues during Spell development, deferring details to subdocuments.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a posture statement with no thresholds, metrics, deadlines, or operative steps. It names roles (Crafter, Spell Reviewer, Core Facilitator) but states no obligation a party could be checked against, and it defers all substance to subdocuments.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph states no consequence, and no cited mechanism reaches a failure to identify or resolve technical issues. Only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops would apply.

assessments.title: Issue Detection and Classification
assessments.quote: When a technical issue is encountered, the party discovering the issue (whether the Crafter, a Reviewer, or another party) must determine whether the issue is either a mistake, a bug, or an exploit. The issue should also be classified as either a result of collusion or a genuine accident. The Spell Team must notify the Core Facilitator of technical issues that require input or adjustments from outside the Spell Team. Note that if a Crafter makes an error in their original development of the Spell, but discovers their own mistake and corrects it before the Reviewers commence the review process, this should not be treated as a technical issue per this handling process.
assessments.description: Requires the discovering party to classify technical issues as mistake, bug, or exploit, and as collusion or accident, and to notify the Core Facilitator when outside input is needed.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligations are real and identifiable, but the classification relies on undefined categories with no criteria for distinguishing mistake, bug, or exploit, or collusion from accident. The notification trigger ('require input or adjustments from outside the Spell Team') and the notification deadline are not quantified.
metrics: Issue must be classified before the Reviewers commence the review process (self-correction carve-out)
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The classification is made by the discovering party, which is self-enforcement, and no cited mechanism (Artifact Review, Emergency Response, or Emergency Spells) is tied to this paragraph's classification or notification duty, so only the generic misalignment backstop would apply.

assessments.title: Issue Analysis and Evidence Capture
assessments.quote: Once a technical issue has been categorized as an instance of a mistake, bug or exploit, the party discovering the issue must prepare documentation of the issue. This generally involves investigating the impacts of the issue, determining how the issue arose, and documenting how the issue manifests. In cases where the issue may be non-technical in nature - such as possible instances of collusion - supporting evidence should be captured, which supports the argument that a non-technical issue may be present. This evidence should be captured in a manner that does not permit bad actors to manipulate or erase the evidence through methods such as editing or deleting messages.
assessments.description: Requires the discovering party to document categorized technical issues and capture evidence of possible non-technical issues tamper-resistantly.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph imposes a real documentation obligation, but its operative language is judgment-based ("generally involves", "should be captured", "manner that does not permit"). It gives no metrics, deadlines, evidence standards, or verification criteria, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No citable mechanism reaches this documentation duty. Artifact review and penalties do not target incident documentation, and the only applicable backstop is the catch-all Reports of Misalignment, which alone is weak. Enforcement: none found.

assessments.title: Determining the Handling Party
assessments.quote: Once a technical issue has been classified and evidence supporting its existence is collected, an entity needs to be designated as the handling party for resolving the issue. This party will typically be the Core Facilitator. However, if there is a non-trivial chance that the Core Facilitator will ignore or downplay the issue, another entity should serve as the handling party.
assessments.description: Requires designating a handling party for technical issues, normally the Core Facilitator, or another entity if the Core Facilitator may downplay the issue.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names a real designation process and default actor, but the override trigger is "non-trivial chance" with no criteria, threshold, or assessment method, so compliance is arguable on the same facts. No deadline or verifiable metric is given.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No contract-enforced control, penalty, or named enforcer reaches the choice of handling party; only the catch-all misalignment and adjudication backstops apply.

assessments.title: Publicly Reporting the Issue
assessments.quote: Discovered issues must be reported publicly unless doing so poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol. Technical issues that are currently or likely to become, actively exploitable must not be discussed in a public manner, as this poses a threat to the security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: Requires public reporting of discovered issues unless disclosure threatens Sky Protocol security, and bars public discussion of exploitable technical issues.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names a real obligation and a security-based exception, but the key triggers ('threat to the security', 'currently or likely to become actively exploitable') are judgment language with no test, cadence, or deadline. A defender could plausibly argue either side of any disclosure decision.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: No catalog mechanism reaches disclosure decisions. Emergency Spells and Liquidity Layer roles do not govern publication. Only the Reports of Misalignment and Adjudication catch-alls apply, so none found.

assessments.title: Resolving the Issue and Following Up
assessments.quote: The Crafter or Reviewer, if they discovered the technical issue, should address or remedy the issue as necessary to resolve it. The handling party (typically the Core Facilitator) must follow up to ensure that the technical issue has been resolved. If the issue poses a threat to the Sky Protocol - such as an exploit or instance of collusion - it should be followed up on as a matter of urgency by the handling party.
assessments.description: Requires the Crafter or Reviewer to remedy discovered technical issues and the handling party to follow up until resolved.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A real obligation exists: the handling party must follow up until the issue is resolved. But the remedy is qualified by "as necessary", the handler is "typically" the Core Facilitator, and urgency is undefined, with no deadline, cadence, or threshold for what counts as a threat.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Core GovOps artifact review (d4bf73e7) can assess whether a spell crafter or reviewer remedied the issue, with penalty assessment, but escalation depends on someone initiating the review. For threats to the protocol, Emergency Spells (b8266c11) plausibly reach an unresolved exploit or collusion, though the paragraph does not link them and no consequence is quantified for this rule.

assessments.title: Issue Retrospective
assessments.quote: Following the resolution of a technical issue, the parties involved in the development process, or other relevant processes leading to the issue arising, must document how the issue arose. These parties (often the Crafter or Reviewer) should also detail any measures that were previously in place to prevent this type of issue occurring, and any measures that can be implemented going forward in order to prevent the same issue from occurring again in the future.
assessments.description: Requires parties involved in a resolved technical issue to document its cause, prior preventive measures, and future prevention steps.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph states a real documentation obligation but uses judgment language such as "often the Crafter or Reviewer" and "any measures". It sets no deadline, format, cadence, or completeness criterion, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, rate limit, role gate, or artifact review in the catalog is shown to reach a failure to write a retrospective, and the only generic backstops (Reports of Misalignment, Adjudication) are catch-all mechanisms that alone are weak.

assessments.title: Spell Team Operational Principles
assessments.quote: As a core member of the Spell Team, the Crafter must comply with the Spell Team Operational Principles throughout their involvement in the Spell development process. These principles apply to both Spell crafting and Spell reviewing processes, and have been included in the documentation of both. These principles are set out in the subdocuments herein.
assessments.description: Requires the Spell Crafter to comply with Spell Team Operational Principles set out in unspecified subdocuments.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph names a regulated actor (the Spell Crafter) but states no metric, threshold, or deadline. The operative principles are deferred to subdocuments that are not included in the text, so there is nothing concrete to comply with here.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No mechanism is tied to this paragraph, and since the principles it requires are undefined in the text, Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) has no criteria to check against. Only the Reports of Misalignment catch-all applies.

assessments.title: Security First
assessments.quote: Any choice between efficiency and security must always be made to maximize security, even at the cost of time, process inefficiency, or gas cost. Smart contract system designs as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always prioritize increased security over increased efficiency, reduced gas cost, or any other benefits. Rules and processes must always maximize security and safety, even at the cost of inefficiency, repetitiveness, longer review or audit timelines, or other drawbacks.
assessments.description: States a principle that security must take precedence over efficiency, gas cost, and timelines in design, code, and processes.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a posture statement with no thresholds, metrics, formulas, deadlines, or verifiable conditions. Compliance cannot be checked from the text, so there is nothing concrete to comply with.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism reaches a generic security-priority principle: artifact review and emergency spells need a specific violation to act on, and the catch-all misalignment and adjudication mechanisms alone are always weak.

assessments.title: Attention to Detail
assessments.quote: Developing, modifying or reviewing code should be done line by line. No change, issue or fix is too minor or unimportant to be commented on or addressed. Sky Core Contracts are immutable, and disabling them often requires waiting for a long period. As such, bugs and exploits should never be present in production code, as they are typically difficult to fix and their presence harms the reputation of the Sky Protocol. Any deployed contract that contains a bug indicates that the existing quality control, auditing, and review processes are not adequately preventing bugs.
assessments.description: Requires line-by-line code review and treats any deployed bug as evidence that quality controls failed.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: A real review obligation exists (line-by-line review, no change too minor to address), but it is expressed in judgment language ("should", "should never") with no metric, cadence, or verifiable threshold. Compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No on-chain control or named enforcer reaches the code-review standard. Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) could plausibly examine spell code quality, but the paragraph does not tie it to a penalty, and the rule's only consequence is the generic misalignment backstop.

assessments.title: Minimizing Complexity
assessments.quote: Smart contract system designs, as well as individual smart contracts, their code, and their interactions must always use a simpler design over a more complex design, unless the more complex design provides a significant net increase to the safety and security of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: Requires smart contract designs and code to use the simpler option unless a more complex design gives a significant net security gain.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule states a directional obligation (prefer simplicity) with an exception, but 'simpler', 'more complex', and 'significant net increase to safety and security' have no metric, measurement method, or threshold. A defender could plausibly argue either compliance or non-applicability on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: Agent Artifact Review By Core GovOps can review spell and contract artifacts with staged findings and penalty assessment, so it plausibly reaches overly complex designs, though no consequence is quantified for this rule and the qualitative standard makes findings arguable.

assessments.title: Lindy-Based Risk Aversion
assessments.quote: The "Lindy Effect" states that the longer something has been in existence in its current state, the longer its remaining life expectancy. The "Lindy" of a system or smart contract refers to the duration it has been operating in its current state and therefore implies its future stability. Specifically, the "Lindy" of immutable systems uses their history of safe and secure operation as a predictor of future safety and security. It is considered best practice to consider the "Lindy" of systems, elements,and smart contracts when evaluating their use or inclusion in the wider system of the Sky Protocol.
assessments.description: States that the operating history (Lindy) of systems and smart contracts should be considered when evaluating their use in Sky Protocol.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The paragraph is a posture statement describing a best practice to 'consider' Lindy. It names no threshold, duration, metric, cadence, or actor-bound obligation that could be verified.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph is a non-binding best-practice statement with no consequence, and no enforcement mechanism in the catalog reaches a duty to consider Lindy.

assessments.title: Chesterton’s Fence
assessments.quote: Chesterton’s Fence is a principle that states that changes must not be made to the current state of affairs unless the reasoning behind the current state of affairs is understood and can be explained. Changes to the Sky Protocol must only be proposed after the context - such as the reasoning, actions, and history - leading to the thing’s current state are known and can be explained by the party proposing the change. Changes must not be approved by team members or otherwise accepted until all parties responsible for overseeing, checking, or reviewing the change are aware of the context behind the current state of affairs as it exists before the change is enacted.
assessments.description: Requires change proposers and reviewers to know and explain the current state's context before proposing or approving changes.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names concrete actors (proposing party, team members, overseers and reviewers) and a timing point (before the change is enacted). The operative standard is judgment language: context must be "known and can be explained" and parties must be "aware", with no defined depth of history, documentation, or test of understanding. A defender could plausibly argue compliance on any given facts.
metrics: Proposer must know and be able to explain the reasoning, actions, and history behind the current state before proposing a change
All responsible overseeing, checking, or reviewing parties must be aware of the pre-change context before approval or acceptance
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. Agent Artifact Review (d4bf73e7) could examine change artifacts but does not test whether the proposer or reviewers understood the historical context, so it does not reach the rule's violation mode. Only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply, and the proposer's self-certification is self-enforcement.

assessments.title: Existing Process Adherence
assessments.quote: All existing Sky processes and patterns, whether pertaining to rules, processes, systems, smart contracts, or code, must be complied with. If regular operation is impossible due to a technical limitation or otherwise, it is permitted so long as it does not compromise the safety or security of the Sky Protocol in any way. New patterns developed in this way must prioritize the safety and security of the Sky Protocol over all other considerations and should be as similar to old patterns as possible. However, deviation from industry norms and best practices is encouraged so long as they are made in the interest of maximizing security. Any deviations by the Crafter or Reviewers must be communicated to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.description: Requires Sky processes to be followed, permits security-preserving deviations, and requires Crafters and Reviewers to report deviations to the Core Facilitator.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: Named actors (Crafter, Reviewers, Core Facilitator) and a reporting duty exist, but the core obligations rely on judgment language such as 'safety or security in any way', 'as similar to old patterns as possible', and 'should'. No threshold, metric, cadence, or deadline for communicating deviations is stated.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No mechanism is tied to this paragraph's compliance or deviation-reporting duties; Reports of Misalignment and Adjudication are catch-all backstops and do not suffice alone, and no emergency or artifact-review path is stated for these deviations.

assessments.title: Tenth Man Mandate
assessments.quote: If a group of people making a decision unanimously holds a certain opinion, all make the same assumption or all come to the same conclusion, it is the responsibility of one member of the group to assume that the rest of the group is incorrect. The member of the group assigned to hold this contrarian viewpoint is referred to as the ‘tenth man’ and must attempt to disprove the group’s decision. Where the ‘tenth man’ is able to provide compelling arguments against the group’s conclusion, the decision must be reassessed.
assessments.description: Requires one group member to argue against unanimous group decisions, and reassess the decision if the counterargument is compelling.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule describes a real procedural obligation (assign a contrarian 'tenth man' to attempt disproof), but it has no numeric threshold, deadline, or defined assigner. 'Compelling arguments' and the process for assigning the role are left to judgment, so compliance is arguable either way.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: none found. No mechanism watches whether a tenth man was assigned or whether the decision was reassessed; the only available backstops are the generic misalignment and adjudication catch-alls, and the group is effectively policing itself.

assessments.title: Providing Voters With Sufficient Information
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that voters have access to sufficient information to make informed decisions. This might include:

- Links to documentation or discussions related to the actions included in the Executive Document.
- Summaries of the actions included in the Executive Document, created by unbiased and knowledgeable third parties.
- Links to any analysis published by DAO-funded entities regarding the actions in the Executive Document.
- Links to well-maintained resources describing the nature of any parameters that may be changed if the Executive Proposal passes.

Providing accessible and complete information is essential to maintaining the legitimacy of the process. Voters should not later regret their vote due to a lack of understanding of the actions they voted on.
assessments.description: Requires the Core Facilitator to give voters sufficient information on Executive Document actions, with examples of possible materials.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation to ensure 'sufficient information' is a real duty, but it is judged entirely by qualitative language ('might include', 'sufficient', 'unbiased', 'well-maintained') with no thresholds, deadlines, or verifiable criteria. Compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No penalty, artifact review, or on-chain control reaches the duty to provide sufficient information; only the generic misalignment and adjudication backstops apply.

assessments.title: Ensuring Transparency And Clarity
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document is clear, transparent, and accessible to all voters. This involves eliminating ambiguity and confusion to the greatest extent possible while balancing technical detail with readability. Voters should clearly understand:

- The effects and impacts of the Executive Vote if passed.
- The processes that led to each item being included in the Executive Document.
- The identities (pseudonymous or entity-level) of those responsible for publishing, writing, and reviewing the Executive Vote.

The goal is to ensure that voters are always provided with information on why an item is included, what will happen if the Executive Vote passes, or who is responsible for its contents.

Clarity reduces the risk of disruption, confusion, or a breakdown of legitimacy in the governance process.

assessments.title: Balancing Technical Detail And Accessibility
assessments.quote:
The Core Facilitator must ensure that the Executive Document balances technical detail with readability. Voters should not require in-depth technical knowledge of the Sky Protocol to understand the Executive Document.
Guidelines for Technical Detail:

- Avoid including excessive technical details that obscure clarity or clutter the Executive Document.
- Include technical details only when they are strictly necessary, such as:
    - In emergency or urgent responses when technical details are the primary focus of the proposal.
    - For non-urgent technical fixes or housekeeping when technical details are relevant, but should be given lower priority compared to other actions in the Executive Vote.

In cases where technical details are included, the Governance Point must ensure they fully understand the technical aspects themselves to present them accurately and clearly.

Excessive technical detail can overwhelm voters and obscure the document's primary purpose. By carefully managing technical content, the Core Facilitator ensures that the document remains accessible and focused.

A defender could argue the document is accessible enough, so compliance is arguable on the same facts.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. No catalog mechanism reaches the readability of an Executive Document. The Executive Vote is a approval step rather than an enforcer of this drafting standard, and the catch-all reporting and adjudication mechanisms alone are weak.

assessments.title: Executive Summary
assessments.quote:
The Executive Summary outlines the key actions that will occur if the proposal passes. It includes:

- The GSM Pause Delay, which specifies the minimum time before the Spell can be executed and is enforced by ds-pause.
- The Office-Hours Modifier, if applicable, which restricts execution to specific times.
- The Expiration Date of the Spell.
    - The Spell must always have an expiration date; it can’t be more than 90 days in the future, and the typical expiration window is 30 days.
- A high-level explanation of the actions being performed in the Spell, presented in bullet-point form.

The summary should provide a high-level overview of the Executive Vote and ensure that SKY holders can quickly understand the scope and purpose of the proposal. This section also explains that voting for the proposal with SKY places support for these actions.

The GSM Pause Delay value is deferred to ds-pause, the Office-Hours Modifier is conditional with no criteria, and the 'high-level explanation' has no defined standard of detail.

    - If the office-hours parameter has the value "Yes" and will be present in the Spell code, this must be explicitly mentioned:

3. Proposal Expiry:
    - The expiry of the proposal must be explicitly noted, including the length of time for which the proposal is valid:
        - "If this Executive Proposal does not pass within 30 days, then it will expire and can no longer have any effect on the Sky Protocol."

assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Validation Window
assessments.quote:
The Ecosystem Spell Validation Window is the period of time during which a Spell can be validated. Validation must occur:

1. After the Spell becomes visible and is available for voting on the Voting Portal (start of the validation window).
2. Before the Spell’s actions become executable, which occurs when the `GSM Pause Delay` elapses (end of the validation window).

Validation outside this window is ineffective because:

- The Spell may still be subject to changes before the start of the validation window.
- The Spell may already be executable after the end of the validation window.

The duration of the validation window is determined by the value of the GSM Pause Delay.
assessments.description: Defines the Spell validation window as running from Voting Portal visibility until the GSM Pause Delay elapses.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The window has concrete event-based start and end triggers (Voting Portal visibility and GSM Pause Delay expiry), but the paragraph states no numeric duration. It delegates the duration to the GSM Pause Delay value, which is not given here, and names no validation threshold or cadence.

Duration equals the value of the GSM Pause Delay (value not stated in paragraph)
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The GSM Pause Delay timelock bounds execution, but no catalogued mechanism penalizes validation outside the window or a missed validation, and the paragraph itself states only that such validation is ineffective.

assessments.title: Ecosystem Spell Verification Scope
assessments.quote:
The scope of Spell validation includes any code in the Sky Protocol that:

1. Must adhere to the `GSM Pause Delay` enforced by the Sky Protocol’s `ds-pause` contract, and
2. Is directly executed by the Sky Protocol’s `Pause Proxy` contract.

Actions that do not meet these criteria—such as `instant actions`, `MOM` and `IAM` contract calls—are excluded from Spell validation.

This exclusion is due to the absence of a pause delay for such actions, which prevents ecosystem actors from having sufficient time to perform their reviews.

Validators should also consider validating the source code or associated audits for contracts added to the Chainlog as part of a Spell, even if these contracts are not immediately executed or fall outside the standard validation scope. This includes pre-deployed emergency Spell contracts, ensuring that their integrity and security are assessed at the time of addition to the Chainlog for potential future use.
assessments.description: Defines which Sky Protocol code falls within Spell validation scope: GSM-delayed code directly executed by Pause Proxy.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The operative scope is a two-part test with named contracts (ds-pause, Pause Proxy) and enumerated exclusions, so a third party can classify most actions. However, the GSM Pause Delay is referenced without a value, and the Chainlog paragraph uses non-binding 'should consider' language.
metrics: GSM Pause Delay adherence (value not stated in this paragraph)
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The ds-pause delay is on-chain, but it constrains spell execution rather than enforcing this validation-scope definition, and no mechanism penalizes Ecosystem Validators for mis-scoping or skipping validation. The Chainlog guidance is advisory.

assessments.title: Spell Validation Checks
assessments.quote:
When validating a Spell, specific checks must be performed to determine whether the Spell passes or fails validation. These checks are categorized into three levels of priority:

- Required Checks: Must be completed for the Spell to pass validation.
- Recommended Checks: Should be completed to ensure best practices, but are not mandatory.
- Additional Checks: Community-developed checks that enhance the validation process.

These checks are detailed in the subdocuments.

assessments.quote: Validators must complete the checks outlined in the subdocuments to be able to determine if a Spell passes or fails validation.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Ensure Tests Pass
assessments.quote:
Ecosystem Spell validators must execute the predefined tests associated with a Spell. These tests are provided as scripts in the Spell repository on GitHub. Validators must run these scripts to verify the correctness, security, and compatibility of the Spell. All tests must pass successfully—without errors or failures—for the Spell to pass validation.

The best practice for running the tests are specified herein:

1. If you haven’t cloned the repository before, run: `git clone <https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/Spells-mainnet`>.
2. Navigate to the Spell repository directory by running: `cd Spells-mainnet`.
3. Update the repository for the latest changes by running: `git pull`.
4. Switch to the correct branch by finding the name from the Spell’s pull request on GitHub, run the command: `git checkout NAME`.
5. Verify your setup and check that you’re on the correct branch by running: `git status`.
6. Clean up old Spell library dependencies by running the command: `rm -r lib` or deleting the `lib` folder and its contents.
7. Install libraries required for the current Spell by running `git submodule update --init --recursive`.
8. Configure the local or remote node being used by running `export ETH_RPC_URL=URL` with the URL of your local or remote node. If using a remote node, do not share the URL as it can be used maliciously.
9. Run the Spell tests by running `make test`. If there are concerns about potential modifications to the function, validators can bypass the `make` command and directly execute the test script using `./scripts/test-dssSpell-forge.sh`.
10. Wait for completion. Allow 20 to 60 minutes for the tests to complete.
11. Review and Save Results: Save the test results (pass or fail) for logging purposes.
assessments.description: Requires Ecosystem Spell validators to run the Spell's repository test scripts and pass all tests before validation.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core pass criterion is objective: all tests must pass without errors or failures. The 20 to 60 minute runtime and the step-by-step commands are concrete, but the steps are framed as 'best practice' and the 'correctness, security, and compatibility' standard is undefined.

Allow 20 to 60 minutes for the tests to complete
Save test results (pass or fail) for logging purposes
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The failing-test outcome gates the Spell, but no mechanism penalizes a validator who skips or misreports test runs. Penalty Mechanisms and Artifact Review target Primes and Agents, not Ecosystem validators, and the Emergency Spells mechanism does not reach test non-execution.

Validators must confirm that the Spell’s smart contract is verified on Etherscan.

Validation can be performed by ensuring that the source code is visible under the "Contract" tab and under "Contract Source Code" on Etherscan. If only bytecode is displayed, the contract is not verified. Additionally, the source must match the correct version in Spells-mainnet on GitHub. A Spell is considered verified if these conditions are met.

assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names an actor and gives objectively checkable conditions: source visible under the Contract tab and Contract Source Code, bytecode-only means unverified, and source must match GitHub. Minor gaps remain: "the correct version" is not pinned to a specific commit or tag, and no verification deadline is stated beyond the Validation Window context.

assessments.quote:
Validators must ensure that the address of the `DssExecLib` library is correct. The correct address corresponds to the latest release as specified in the `DssExecLib` GitHub repository. The deployed Spell must use and display the correct `DssExecLib` address on Etherscan to pass validation.

The validation can be performed by navigating to the "Libraries Used" section on the "Contract tab" on Etherscan. The library address displayed there must be compared against the official address specified in the README file ([https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/dss-exec-lib?tab=readme-ov-file#dss-exec-library](https://github.com/sky-ecosystem/dss-exec-lib?tab=readme-ov-file#dss-exec-library)) of the `DssExecLib` GitHub repository.

It names the actor (validators), the source of truth, and the pass condition. The minor gap is that 'latest release' is not pinned to a version or date, so a README lag could create ambiguity.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Code
assessments.quote:
The Spell validator must ensure that the deployed Spell code matches the Spell code present in the GitHub Repository.

In order to pass validation, the deployed Spell must not contain any potentially malicious code or any notable functional changes within the `DssSpellAction`.

The validation for the Spell code can be done by using the `diff-deployed-Spell` script present in the Spell repository on GitHub to ensure that the deployed Spell’s code matches locally compiled code. Alternatively, an online tool like diff checker ([https://www.diffchecker.com/](https://www.diffchecker.com/)) can be used. The Spell code on Etherscan should be compared with the `DssSpell.sol` in the GitHub repository for the relevant Spell. If the Spell goes live before the code is merged to the main branch, it’s possible to find the branch by the Target Date name of the Spell (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD).

When comparing, note that the following differences are acceptable and should not be flagged (based on validation guides):

- Comments: Lines starting with `//` or inside `/* */`.
- Imports and Solidity versions: Multiple declarations in the GitHub code.
- Interfaces: Numerical suffixes like `_1` or `_2` added to interface names in the contract.
- DssExecLib Interface: Extra code or warnings within the `DssExecLib` library.
assessments.description: Requires Spell validators to confirm deployed Spell code matches the GitHub repository and contains no malicious or notable functional changes.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names an actor (Spell validator), concrete checking procedures (the diff-deployed-Spell script, diffchecker, Etherscan comparison), and an enumerated list of acceptable differences. The pass criterion for 'potentially malicious code' or 'notable functional changes' is qualitative, with no defined threshold.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) can freeze a threatened spell, but they do not reach a validator's failure to perform the check. Ecosystem validators face no penalty, artifact review, or insurance repricing tied to this duty, so only the misalignment catch-all applies.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Is Not A DarkSpell
assessments.quote:
Validators must confirm that the deployed Spell does not execute an external `DssAction` contract. This validation ensures that the Spell is self-contained, does not rely on external contracts or pre-defined Ethereum addresses, and that the `DssExec` and `DssSpellAction` contracts are deployed together and not separately, as is done when using DarkSpells. Validators must perform the following two checks:

1. Check that the DssAction contract’s `execute()` function only calls the `actions()` function and does not interact with any external contracts or explicitly defined Ethereum addresses.
2. Check that the second argument used in the constructor when instantiating the `DssExec` is a newly created Spell action contract (e.g. `address(new DssSpellAction())`) and not an explicitly defined Ethereum address. This confirms that the Spell is linked to the correct action contract.

If either of these checks fails, the Spell cannot pass validation.

The validation checks can be performed by navigating to the "Contract tab" on Etherscan for the deployed Spell. In the source code, first locate the `DssAction` contract (or its equivalent, such as `DssSpellAction`). Review the `execute()` function and make sure that it only calls the `actions()` function. Then, locate the constructor and confirm that the `action` argument is instantiated as a new contract.
assessments.description: Requires validators to confirm a deployed Spell's DssAction is self-contained, with no external contract calls or hardcoded addresses.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: Two binary, checkable conditions are stated with a defined actor (validators), a procedure, and a pass/fail outcome. The phrases "interact with any external contracts" and "explicitly defined Ethereum addresses" leave some interpretive room, and there is no cadence.

DssExec constructor second argument is a newly created Spell action contract (e.g. address(new DssSpellAction())), not an explicit address
assessments.enforcementReasoning: The rule is a pre-execution gate: a failed check means the Spell cannot pass validation, but enforcement depends on validators performing the checks. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) could freeze or pause a malicious Spell that slipped through validation, which plausibly reaches this violation mode, but escalation is not automatic.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Was Not Deployed Using CREATE2
assessments.quote:
Validators must ensure that no contract, neither the Spell Executive contract (DssSpell / DssExec) nor the Spell Action contract (DssSpellAction / DssAction) - was deployed using the `CREATE2` opcode.

To perform this validation, the validator must:

- Locate and copy the contract creation transaction on Etherscan. The contract creation transaction can be found under the "internal transactions" tab on Etherscan.
- Use a transaction decoder, such as Tenderly or another blockchain analysis tool, to decode the transaction hash and identify the opcode used during deployment.
- Ensure the opcode is `CREATE`. If `CREATE2` is used, the Spell fails validation.
assessments.description: Requires validators to confirm the Spell Executive and Spell Action contracts were deployed with CREATE, not CREATE2, by inspecting the creation transaction's opcode.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The obligation is a binary, verifiable check with a named actor (validators), defined steps, and a pass/fail outcome (CREATE required, CREATE2 fails). Gaps: no cadence, the "another blockchain analysis tool" is open-ended, and it does not say how the opcode is read from the decoder output.

Spell fails validation if CREATE2 is used

No catalog mechanism (penalty, conservatorship, rate limiter, role gating, artifact review) reaches a validator's failure to check or a spell's CREATE2 deployment, so none found; the rating rests on the generic misalignment backstop.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell Optimization Settings
assessments.quote:
Validators must ensure that the code optimization settings used by the Spell contract are correct.
Validators should ensure the following:

- The `Optimization Enabled` field on Etherscan is set to `No with 200 runs` unless explicitly required due to contract size constraints during deployment.
- If optimization is enabled, the value of the `Optimization Enabled` must be `Yes with 200 runs` unless the optimization settings have been specified in the Instruction Document as a specific number of runs, which must be a multiple of 100 other than 0.
- If the optimization settings are incorrect (e.g., `No with 13767 runs` or `Yes with 0 runs`), the Spell fails validation.

To perform this validation, the validator must go to the contract tab on Etherscan and review the `Optimization Enabled` field under the contract’s metadata.

assessments.precisenessReasoning: The core obligation is quantified: optimization must read 'No with 200 runs' by default or 'Yes with 200 runs', with run counts that are multiples of 100 and never 0. Gaps remain in the 'contract size constraints' exception, the Instruction Document override, and the 'should' versus 'must' wording.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell EVM Version
assessments.quote:
Validators must ensure that the correct EVM version for the Spell contract is displayed on Etherscan. The EVM version is determined by the Solidity compiler version used during compilation. For the Spell to pass validation, the `Other Settings` field on Etherscan must display either "Default" or the correct default EVM version name for that compiler release (e.g., for Solidity 0.8.16, either "Default" or "London" is acceptable, as London is the default EVM for that compiler version).

To perform this validation, the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the `Other Settings` field under the contract’s metadata.

Compliance is verifiable from the text, though the correct default EVM for each compiler release must be looked up externally and no cadence is given.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Perform Basic Spell Code Validation
assessments.quote:
The Spell validator must perform a brief review of the Spell code. This includes reviewing the `DssSpellAction` contract within the `DssSpell.sol` file.

Validators should look for any unusual behavior, such as:

- Low-level assembly operations (e.g., `assembly` blocks).
- The use of Solidity opcodes, such as `delegatecall`, `callcode`, or `selfdestruct`.
- Suspicious-looking payments or transfers.
- Any other malicious or unauthorized code. This includes cross-checking the Solidity code in `actions()` against the Executive Sheet and the Executive Document. Each action must be authorized per the Atlas.

Spell validators must report any code they find that appears to be malicious or which likely forms part of an attempted attack. A Spell must not pass validation if the Spell validator is convinced that malicious code is present in a Spell or that its execution can lead to an attack on the Sky Protocol.

To perform this validation, the validator must go to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and review the source code.
assessments.description: Requires Spell validators to briefly review DssSpellAction code for malicious or unusual patterns, and to block spells they find dangerous.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule names a concrete actor, file, and Etherscan tab and lists specific opcodes, but the operative standards are judgment language: "brief review", "unusual behavior", "appears to be malicious", and "convinced". Compliance could be argued either way on the same facts, and no time or depth threshold is set.
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found that enforces validator duties directly. The only consequence is that a spell "must not pass validation", which is self-gated by the validator. Emergency Spells (b8266c11) could respond to a malicious spell but do not penalize a validator who fails to review or report, and the misalignment catch-all alone is weak.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Deployed Spell License
assessments.quote:
The correct license for the Spell contract is GNU AGPLv3. Validators should confirm that this license is used, which can be verified in one of two ways under the "Contract" tab on Etherscan:

1. In the `Other Settings` field under the contract’s metadata. The license should be displayed as `GNU AGPLv3`.
2. In the Spell Code in the commented line of code in the `DssSpell` contract. The line should contain: `SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-or-later`.

While the Spell should use the correct license to pass validation, this is not considered a strict requirement.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Must Check Compiler Version
assessments.quote:
Validators should ensure that the Solidity compiler version used in the deployed Spell matches the version specified in the `Spells-mainnet` repository on GitHub. Validators should verify this by:

- Navigate to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and check the `Compiler Version` field under the contract’s metadata. The version displayed must match the version specified in the `DssSpell.sol` contract (e.g., pragma solidity `0.8.16`;).
- Only the first part of the version (e.g., `v0.8.16`) needs to match; any additional commit information can be ignored.

While the Spell should use the correct version to pass validation, this is not considered a strict requirement.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Validate Executive Document
assessments.quote:
The Spell validator should confirm that the smart contract developers referenced the correct governance copy when building the Spell and that the document voters see on the Voting Portal matches the Spell contents. This is done by verifying that the hash in the Spell corresponds to the version of the Executive Document stored in the GitHub repository.

To perform this validation, the validator must first locate the Executive Hash, which can be found on the voting platform under "Spell Details" for the Executive Vote. Validators should be aware that the hash refers to an earlier commit of the Executive Document markdown, prior to the inclusion of the contract address. After validating the hash against this earlier commit, validators must conduct a diff check between the commit associated with the Executive Hash and the final version of the document to confirm that the only difference is the replacement of the Spell address placeholder.

The check can be performed in two ways:

1. Using an Online Tool:
    - Copy and paste the body of the Executive Document from GitHub into the online Keccak-256 hash generator tool ([https://emn178.github.io/online-tools/keccak_256.html](https://emn178.github.io/online-tools/keccak_256.html)).
    - Compare the generated hash with the hash included in the Spell.
2. Using `cast`
    - Generate the hash directly from the raw GitHub URL at the specific commit:
        - Run the following command to generate the hash: `cast keccak -- "$(wget $RAW_EXEC_URL -O -)"`
        - Use the raw file URL at the specific commit.
    - Compare the generated hash with the hash included in the Spell.
assessments.description: Requires Spell validators to match the Spell's executive hash to a GitHub commit and confirm only the address placeholder differs.
assessments.precisenessReasoning: The rule gives concrete verification steps: Keccak-256 hashing, a binary hash-equality check, a diff limited to the Spell address placeholder, and a specific cast command. A third party could test compliance from the text. It lacks a deadline or cadence and does not say what a validator must do on mismatch.
metrics: Generated Keccak-256 hash must match the hash included in the Spell
Diff between the Executive Hash commit and final document must show only replacement of the Spell address placeholder
assessments.enforcementReasoning: None found. The paragraph sets no penalty, rejection, or escalation for a validator who skips or misreports the check. No on-chain mechanism reverts a missed validation, and the only reachable path is the misalignment and adjudication catch-alls, which are weak on their own.

assessments.title: Spell Validators Should Review Spell Constructor
assessments.quote:
Validators should ensure that the Spell constructor is properly implemented. The constructor is a critical part of the Spell contract, as it defines key parameters such as the Spell's expiry time and the inclusion of the `DssSpellAction` code block, which specifies the actions the Spell will execute.

Validators should follow these steps to review the constructor:

- Navigate to the "Contract" tab on Etherscan and scroll to the bottom of the contract source code to locate the constructor declaration.
    - Verify that the Spell inherits from the `DssExec` contract, which serves as the base contract for all Sky Spells.
    - Verify that the constructor is properly implemented with the correct parameters. For example, the expiry time should be set to the correct duration (e.g., `30 days`).
assessments.description: Requires Ecosystem Validators to check the Spell constructor on Etherscan for DssExec inheritance and correct parameters.

Magnitudes are delegated to the reviewer's judgment.

Validators should ensure that all values before and after the Spell actions are constants or immutable. If values are not constants, they could present malicious code in the form of memory mutations impacting the function of the pause proxy.

Spell validators should ensure that all `DssExecLib` calls to the chainlog use the correct name descriptors.

- Confirm that the name descriptors match the expected values as recorded in the Chainlog.
